item.title: Be Like Buddha, See Moods Like the Weather
item.description:
Emotions

Be Like Buddha, See Moods Like the Weather

We can be impartial about moods and see through our desires, 看破 kàn pò.

Posted June 25, 2026

Key points
  • Emotional detachment and adopting an objective, non-critical perspective might reduce the discomfort we feel.
  • Anxiety rates in the U.S. are higher than in other nations.
  • Some people have a fear of happiness as well as a degree of emotional numbness.

Some Chinese refer to emotional detachment as seeing through, 看破 kàn pò, our desires and materialism. It is the emotional detachment where one is not upset by circumstances, all of which are temporary. Certainly, complete emotional immobilization is decidedly harmful, but detachment can be good. The Buddha might approve. And there is evidence that one can feel more neutral and less charged about emotional events. In one study, Japanese participants reported struggling with emotions less often than Americans do. In another study from the journal Emotion, Japanese subjects, when compared with American subjects, were found to feel more mixed emotions about pleasant situations; having such mixed emotions could be another form of detachment.

Source: AI Generated

In other cultures around the world, feeling uncomfortable is just a part of normal living. When we confront a problem, we may want to blame ourselves, but removing the self from the equation could be helpful. We may be inclined to ask, “What is the matter with me?” We can instead ask, “What is wrong with the scenario I am in?” or “How do I handle this difficult situation?”

People see moods differently in other cultures. About four in 10 Americans experience anxiety or depression, according to a Kaiser Family Foundation report. However, island nations like the Solomons and Papua New Guinea have among the lowest rates of depression at 3 percent or lower, according to the stats organization Data Pandas.

Happiness Can Be Fragile

Research has looked into this fragility—a sort of fear of happiness state of mind—whereby a person thinks that clutching at happiness is a bad objective because awful things are always coming at us. Being miserable is what the person knows.

For these people, happy times may seem like a trap. They may even be skeptical of bliss and suffer from the inability to enjoy pleasure, called anhedonia. They are more comfortable with tragedy, trauma, and misery. In the end, they seem unable to reach the solid ground of contentment. If every person has the potential to break your heart, they might argue, why bother reaching out to others for real connection?

They may be able to access their feelings, but they may not allow themselves to feel good. They may think, I do not deserve to feel happy. They may think they have no right to experience compassion in any form, especially self-compassion. They may then waive happiness for hardened strength to give the impression that they can bear and withstand any difficulty—they are not frail. For some people, this tendency may be entrenched because they were dismissed or neglected by caretakers during their younger years.

In extreme cases, anhedonia can be a symptom of depression and other conditions like bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress. French psychologist Théodule Ribot described l’anhédonie, or the disappearance of pleasure, in 1896 as the opposite of l’analgésie, the absence of pain.

The Inability to Feel

In other cases, some people suffer from alexithymia. While not a disorder, this suite of features highlights a person’s inability to recognize and feel their emotions, with empathy particularly hard to come by. A person with alexithymia may even be misdiagnosed with autism. If they feel discomfort and psychic pain, they may engage in behaviors to make that discomfort disappear. These behaviors may include impulsivity, emotional eating, binge drinking, or other self-destructive actions like self-mutilation.

Coined in the 1970s by psychiatrist Peter Sifneos, alexithymia is derived from Greek and means having no words for emotions. Approximately 12 percent of people have this trait, and individuals with alexithymia are more vulnerable to mental disorders, especially depressive ones. When a person with alexithymia is under mental and or physical duress, they are more likely to say, “I am fine.” They think they are fine because accessing emotions is not possible for them. The feeling of joy is likewise demobilized. If they do not know how to feel, they do not know how to feel good.

While most people do not suffer extreme cases of anhedonia or alexithymia, some people have a fear of happiness as well as a degree of emotional numbness. When we experience, for example, the end of a painful relationship, we prefer not to ever live through that hurt again. Arming ourselves with emotional numbness sounds fine. However, this only works for the time being. Ideally, after grieving the end of a relationship, we can learn from it and move on to a better one the next time around.

Our negative mood states do not have to hamper or immobilize us. Certainly, modern-day living can handicap us and make us feel like we are failures. However, we don’t have to be distorted by our expectations and how we see ourselves. The alternative is preferable. If we think about moods differently, we can learn from our mistakes and disappointments. Instead of caving in the face of a setback, we can let the brain rewire itself, and our difficult experiences can inform us. Viewing our moods with less involvement can help us out of misery.

item.title: When Does a "Personality Hire" Truly Matter?
item.description:
Personality

When Does a "Personality Hire" Truly Matter?

Likability, confidence, and social ease can displace essential job criteria.

Posted June 25, 2026

Key points
  • Nearly half of workers view themselves as "personality hires," making the term mainstream.
  • Extraverted, confident candidates enjoy advantages in roles that rely on influence and public engagement.
  • While social fluency is often useful, demonstrating ease in interviews often gets mistaken for job competence.

The phrase “personality hire” has become a recognizable part of workplace language. In a recent Monster survey, 48 percent of workers said they saw themselves that way. That alone suggests the term is no longer fringe. It has become a mainstream way of describing a familiar hiring reality: Some people are chosen not only for what they can do, but for how they make other people feel.

At one level, this makes perfect sense. Most jobs are not performed in isolation. People work in teams, interact with clients, manage tension, communicate under pressure, and help shape the emotional tone of a workplace. In that context, interpersonal presence is not trivial. A person who can build trust quickly, lower friction, steady a room, or make collaboration easier may contribute something genuinely valuable. Employers are not wrong to care about that.

In some roles, interpersonal effect is not secondary to performance; it is part of performance. A person who reassures anxious clients, helps a team communicate more smoothly, or creates an atmosphere of ease may be contributing something substantive, not merely decorative. The rise of the “personality hire” may reflect a more open acknowledgment of that reality.

At the same time, the phrase points to a real psychological risk. Human beings are quick to convert ease of interaction into a broader judgment of merit. The person who seems comfortable, confident, and likable can easily come across as more capable than the person who is quieter, less polished, or slower to warm up. Social ease can begin to stand in for competence.

This is one reason the topic is so interesting psychologically. A “personality hire” is not just a trendy label. It highlights a longstanding tension in social judgment: the difference between the person who feels good to be around and the person who will actually perform best.

Warmth vs. Competence: Two Ways to Judge Job Seekers

Research on first impressions helps explain why this happens. Social psychologists have long argued that warmth and competence are two of the main dimensions that people use to evaluate others. Warmth includes qualities like friendliness, sincerity, and likability. Competence includes qualities like intelligence, skill, and effectiveness. In everyday life, these dimensions often blur together. Someone who is verbally smooth, relaxed, and socially adept can quickly be perceived as more competent than they really are, especially in brief, high-stakes settings like job interviews.

The interview is especially vulnerable to this bias because it is not just an assessment of what a person knows. It is also a social encounter. Interviewers respond not only to the content of a candidate’s answers, but to the impression the candidate creates. Does this person seem easy to talk to? Self-assured? Polished? Likely to fit in? Those impressions can form quickly, and once formed, they can shape the rest of the evaluation.

Research by Barrick and colleagues found that interviewers’ initial impressions during the rapport-building stage of an interview were strongly related to how they later evaluated candidates’ answers, even in structured interviews. That means early social impressions don’t simply sit in the background. They can influence how later evidence is interpreted.

Extraversion appears to play a role here as well. Research has shown that extraverted applicants tend to use more self-promotion in interviews, which can shape recruiters' perceptions of fit and similarity. In practical terms, people who are more comfortable projecting energy and confidence may have an advantage in settings where social fluency is highly visible.

That does not mean hiring for personality is inherently misguided. It means organizations may be trying to select for two different things at once: job-relevant interpersonal strengths and a more general feeling of rapport. Sometimes those overlap. Sometimes they don’t. A candidate may genuinely bring social value to a role. But a candidate may also simply be easier to imagine succeeding because they are socially fluent in the interview itself.

This is where the phrase becomes ambiguous. Calling someone a “personality hire” can sound dismissive, as though their social strengths came at the expense of substance. But it can also recognize that workplaces depend on more than technical ability alone. Some people truly are hired in part because they create trust, cohesion, ease, or momentum, and those effects can matter.

The survey data reinforce that this is not just a passing insult. If nearly half of workers now see the label as applying to them, the phrase seems to be capturing something real about how people understand hiring today. The question is not whether personality matters. It clearly does. The more important question is when interpersonal strengths are being recognized appropriately—and when they are being used as a shortcut for qualities that have not yet been demonstrated.

The Real Role of Social Fluency in the Workplace

One of the most durable findings in industrial-organizational psychology is that conscientiousness is a relatively consistent predictor of job performance across occupations. Extraversion matters too, but more selectively, especially in jobs that rely heavily on interaction, influence, or public engagement. In many roles, the quieter qualities of reliability, follow-through, judgment, and steady execution matter at least as much as visible charisma—and often more.

This helps explain why the rise of the “personality hire” has generated mixed reactions. It captures something true: Personality does matter at work. But it also exposes how easily social fluency can be mistaken for broader merit. The very traits that make someone memorable in an interview may not be the same traits that matter most once the day-to-day work begins.

Research on interviews offers one practical lesson. Structured interviews, which use standardized questions and scoring, predict job performance better than unstructured interviews. The more a hiring process depends on gut feeling, chemistry, and overall vibe, the more room there is for social ease to overshadow slower, less visible forms of competence.

What the rise of the “personality hire” really reveals, then, is not simply that employers like socially engaging people. It reveals that workplaces are not just choosing workers. They are choosing social presences. The challenge is to know when that presence is a genuine part of the job—and when it is simply making competence easier to imagine than to verify.

Seen in that light, the phrase is less trivial than it sounds. It reflects a real shift in workplace language, but also a much older truth about human judgment. We are drawn to people who make interaction feel smooth. We infer competence from confidence. We trust what feels effortless.

Sometimes that instinct leads us toward genuinely strong candidates, but other times it may reward polish over substance.

item.title: Exploring the Experience and Benefits of Caffeinated Coffee
item.description:
Cognition

Exploring the Experience and Benefits of Caffeinated Coffee

Research shows caffeinated coffee may protect against dementia.

Posted June 25, 2026

Key points
  • Coffee's aroma and taste involve over a thousand compounds with varied sensory pathways.
  • Moderate caffeinated coffee intake is linked to an 18% lower risk of dementia.
  • Only caffeinated, not decaf, coffee or tea is associated with decreased dementia risk.

It’s not uncommon to encounter someone who likes the aroma of coffee but has never adapted themselves to the habit of drinking it. “I love the smell of fresh-ground coffee, especially in the morning, but I don’t like the taste,” is a typical self-description.

This distinction between smell and taste depends on an array of anatomical, biological, and chemical factors. While taste and smell are clearly intertwined—the sudden loss of taste for gourmet dinners is often the first symptom of COVID-19—there are major differences.

First—sticking to coffee—both the flavor and smell are the result of a complex cocktail of more than a thousand compounds. The balance of flavors is modified by varying factors: what beans are selected and how long they are roasted, as well as variations in the brewing methods, such as temperature and pressure. Any one of these contributors can affect how many of the harder-to-extract flavors emanate from that morning cuppa. Of the different flavors, some are more easily vaporized than others, allowing them to diffuse through the air and enter your nose, where you initially smell them. Other flavor compounds are larger and need higher temperatures to vaporize—you smell them less, or not at all.

In addition, we smell coffee via two different pathways. The orthonasal path located in the nose detects external aromas within the environment. The more volatile aromatics are detectable in the air emanating from the coffee beans blended within the brew. The retronasal route picks up aromas from the back of the mouth and pulses them into the nose whenever we are eating or drinking.

No matter how much sugar and cream you add to it, coffee has a predominantly bitter taste. And that is the problem: We possess an inborn aversion to bitter taste, probably thanks to our ancestors' aversion to alkaloid toxins: the substances that protect plants from being eaten.

Thanks to conditioning, most of us learned to accept coffee’s bitterness because of the pick-me-up associated with an early morning cup of joe. But there are exceptions: I never picked up the coffee habit until I was recovering from an illness that robbed me of my energy. Initially, I took it as a medicinal energizer, but I soon developed a liking for it.

But developing a liking for coffee isn’t simply based on a desire to overcome fatigue at the cost of passively accepting the brew’s inherent bitterness. Coffee gives off hundreds of volatile flavors that are perceived as pleasant aromas—its “chocolate notes,” for instance.

Another point: None of the one thousand or so different volatiles in isolation is responsible for the smell of coffee, nor do all of the individual components arouse a pleasant sensation. Indole, for instance, has a strongly fecal smell, but you are unlikely to perceive it concealed within the general coffee aroma unless you are pregnant. Pregnancy increases sensitivity to coffee components that may possibly be harmful. The sensitivity to indole varies among pregnant women according to the stage of the pregnancy and ceases—either gradually or suddenly—when the woman is no longer pregnant. Similarly, more common changes in background physiology (hunger, fatigue, excitability, even something like a “hangover”) shape how a smell is perceived. “This astonishing variety in the perception effectively corresponds to differences in the sensitivity of your olfactory receptors,” according to Ann Sophie Barish, author of Smellosophy.

In summary, odor appreciation can vary not only among different people but also within the same person under different conditions and circumstances. Thus, the smell receptors are not rigid and unchangeable (often compared to locks that accommodate the different keys representing different odorants) but dynamically mutating chemical arrangements.

How Caffeine Affects the Brain

Surprisingly, the effects of coffee on the brain aren’t all that complicated. Caffeine’s primary action is blocking adenosine receptors. Adenosine is the chemical that builds up in the brain during waking hours, and its gradual accumulation leads to drowsiness and eventually sleep. With the blocking of the adenosine receptors by coffee, a person feels less fatigued, more alert, and invigorated. Caffeine also indirectly influences other neurotransmitters, such as dopamine, acetylcholine, and norepinephrine, which improve vigilance and mental performance.

As any coffee drinker will tell you, caffeinated coffee facilitates attention, makes “boring tasks” less boring, quickens reaction time, improves learning, and, as a consequence, strengthens memory.

Research on Caffeinated Coffee and Dementia

Along with all of these benefits, recent research strongly suggests that moderate consumption of caffeinated coffee lessens the risk of dementia. That conclusion was based on two studies: The Nurses’ Health Study, comprising more than 86,000 participants from 1980 to 2023, and the Health Professionals Follow-Up Study with more than 45,000 male participants followed from 1996 to 2023.

Members of these two groups ranked their coffee, tea, or caffeine consumption. Among the highest coffee drinkers, females drank a median of 4.5 cups of coffee a day, with men clocking in at 2.5 cups a day. After more than 43 years of follow-up, higher consumption of caffeinated coffee led to an 18 percent lower dementia risk.

Higher caffeinated coffee consumption was also associated with better subjective cognitive performance (probably a reflection of coffee’s alerting and focusing effects), compared to study participants who guzzled down little or no caffeinated coffee. Increased caffeinated tea consumption showed similar cognitive outcomes. But consuming “no caffeine” coffee or tea did not bestow any benefit in terms of decreasing the likelihood of dementia. “The most pronounced differences were observed with intake of approximately two to three cups per day of caffeinated coffee, or one or two cups per day of caffeinated tea,” according to Daniel (Dong) Wang, a senior author of the study.

So, based on the combined findings of two studies, should you start drinking coffee if you haven’t imbibed thus far in your life? Although it is a personal decision, you should discuss it with your physician. If there are no health contraindications, consider this: Taking up the coffee habit provides you with an additional weapon in your armamentarium against dementia: Coffee serves as a worthy accompaniment to increased physical and intellectual activity, along with all of the other now-recognized factors that promote cognitive health.

item.title: Understanding Passive Aggression and Schadenfreude
item.description:
Schadenfreude

Understanding Passive Aggression and Schadenfreude

Knowing the difference helps us determine where we put energy or action.

Posted June 25, 2026

Key points
  • Passive aggression is indirect action; schadenfreude is hidden pleasure at others' misfortune.
  • Hostility can play a role in both passive aggression and schadenfreude.
  • Assertiveness is the balanced choice between passivity and aggression, aiding problem-solving.

While passive aggression, rooted in hidden anger and resentment, involves a communication style that’s indirect,1 silent, or shown through blatant inactivity, schadenfreude is an emotion or feeling that does not come forward in action or lack of it.

Let’s say you’ve been tormented by a bullying co-worker. Suddenly, it’s time for performance reviews, and there’s even a departmental promotion that several, including this co-worker, covet.

You see your co-worker leave the boss’s office frustrated. Later that day, it’s announced that another colleague has gotten the nod, the coveted position. You are thrilled that your office tormentor did not prevail.

Experiencing pleasure or joy from someone’s disappointments, humiliations, or other troubles is classic schadenfreude. Deriving pleasure from pain you’ve inflicted on another might also have shades of sadism. However, that’s a darker personality issue where the perpetrator has a desire for dominance or power.

Schadenfreude was adopted from the German combination of schaden, meaning damage or harm, and freude, meaning joy or pleasure. Literally, it translates to “harm-joy,” and Emory researchers have identified a dehumanization aspect to it as well.2 In today’s parlance, we describe schadenfreude more as a phrase, such as gloating over misfortune or armchair malice, versus a single-word synonym, such as epicaricacy.

This ancient Greek word means the same; it’s so obscure to be barely recognized in English. (And no, the word schadenfreude has nothing to do with Sigmund Freud, the Austrian neurologist and founder of psychoanalysis.)

Can Schadenfreude and Passive Aggression Exist Together?

Yes, indeed, but not always. Here’s an example:

Let’s say you’re on vacation, running behind due to a late flight that made you miss a train connection in a foreign country. The last available tickets get you to the train station at midnight, so you thoughtfully reserve a ride through a well-known ride-share/ride-hailing service, where all arrangements and communication are app-driven.

Upon arrival, you’re time-focused, thus you screenshot the app directions to the pick-up point. You communicate with the driver that you’ve arrived, and you’re heading to the designated spot. The driver, for whatever reason, becomes petulant and demands you meet at the opposite side of the station.

You message that you’ve got luggage, and this would take more time. You think you’re being helpful as you describe your appearance, the pick-up point, and message the screenshotted directions.

Abruptly, the driver cancels on you—after midnight, in a foreign country where potentially your grasp of the language is phrase-based at best. What’s more, you soon find that the company has disabled your account because this driver reported himself as the victim of a “verbal altercation.” You’re even more gobsmacked since you never actually spoke. Now, you’re really inconvenienced.

Exploring Bad Behaviors and Bad Actors

Sadly, the scenario posed is based on a real-life experience; though, for privacy, I’ve not disclosed names. It could happen to anyone, especially during travel, on holidays, or business trips.

To be more certain that behavior meets passive-aggressive standards, motive and outcome ought both be negative. We don’t have an absolute window—only clues—into the motives. Indeed, most ride-hailing companies insist drivers keep cancellation rates below four to five percent, or it’s a red flag that doesn’t bode well.

Facts point to creating a false narrative (lying), shirking work-related responsibility (passive-aggression there), and manipulation (the same).

If both motive and outcome are negative, the driver intended to inconvenience because he saw a better opportunity, didn’t care that the ride was reserved ahead of time or about the time involved, was plain lazy on the job, or worst case, had poor personality traits previously described, then yes, all three could occur—passive-aggression (setting up a situation and acting indirectly), schadenfreude (feeling glee at the inconvenience), and sadism (if there was a quest to dominate a situation and power felt over that orchestration). Yet, if you remove features from this context, then you can see that the behaviors would be more isolated.

According to Alison Baren, who wrote a dissertation on why people take pleasure in others’ misfortune, whether people are in competitive or cooperative situations is relevant. She reviewed how people’s feelings of hostility trigger schadenfreude. People who score higher in the dark triad traits exhibit less prosocial behavior.3 In interpersonal relationships, Baren explored attachment theory, which would apply more in interpersonal relations, not those with strangers.

Protecting Oneself Against Harmful Behaviors

In this true scenario, the ride-hailing company reached out for the customer's version of the story when it informed her that her account was disabled. Having the app’s directions, which she tried her best to follow, helped her case. She had also remembered the driver’s name. She had not taken a screenshot or saved their conversation, which was erased when the driver canceled. Thankfully, her account was restored, and apologies were extended, possibly as management saw the corroborating communication on a back channel.

When the consumer spotted a charge for the cancellation upon her return, she took it up with the company, again with her facts, and now, the restoration email. That assertiveness skill earned her a refund. But what a literal and emotional hassle!

Indeed, pack your patience, your best planning in all situations, but especially when you’re in more vulnerable situations. If you’re traveling with others, be sure that they have access to such ride services at the ready. If you’re alone, be sure to have researched alternative transportation means. Our traveler here was not alone and thankfully spotted one remaining taxi to get them to their hotel in the wee hours.

Assertiveness is worth cultivating as a preventative measure. “Being assertive means that you act in your best interests without violating others’ rights … Assertiveness equates to being firm but tactful, and it conveys openness, problem solving, compromise and negotiation,” I wrote in Overcoming Passive-Aggression.3 Assertiveness is appropriate, in the middle of a spectrum which include passivity on one end and aggression on the other; neither of those being helpful choices in most situations.

item.title: What Does Emotional Safety Actually Feel Like?
item.description:
Relationships

What Does Emotional Safety Actually Feel Like?

Why many people recognize danger more easily than emotional safety.

Posted June 25, 2026

Key points
  • Emotional safety is more than the absence of conflict or danger.
  • Many people are highly trained to recognize threats but struggle to recognize safety.
  • Emotional attunement helps create safety in relationships.
  • Safety often feels quieter than anxiety and uncertainty and may initially be mistaken for boredom.

In my work as a psychologist and sex therapist, I often hear people say they want safety in their romantic relationships. They want a partner who is trustworthy, emotionally available, and consistent. They want to feel secure, connected, and at ease. But when I ask what safety actually feels like, many people struggle to answer.

Most people can quickly identify what does not feel safe. They know what criticism feels like. They know what emotional withdrawal feels like. They know what it is like to walk on eggshells, worry about upsetting someone, or wonder whether a relationship could disappear at any moment. They know the experience of analyzing a text message, reading it multiple times, and looking for signs that something is wrong. They know the experience of sensing a shift in someone's mood and immediately wondering if they caused it.

Safety, however, is often harder to recognize. One reason is that many of us become highly skilled at detecting danger long before we learn how to recognize safety. If you grew up in an environment where connection felt inconsistent, where moods shifted unexpectedly, where criticism was common, or where your emotional needs were overlooked, your nervous system likely adapted by becoming more alert. That alertness served an important purpose. It helped you navigate your environment and maintain connection in whatever ways were available to you. That alertness can also be called an “insecure attachment style,” and research continues to show that attachment patterns are closely tied to how adults regulate emotions, perceive relationships, and respond to experiences of closeness and vulnerability.1,2

The challenge is that a nervous system organized around monitoring for threat does not automatically know how to recognize safety. As adults, many people continue scanning relationships for signs of disappointment, rejection, criticism, or withdrawal. They become experts in noticing what might go wrong. But when they encounter steadiness, predictability, and genuine care, those experiences can feel unfamiliar. Sometimes they even feel boring, suspicious, or difficult to trust.

This is one reason emotionally healthy relationships can feel confusing at first. Many people assume safety should feel obvious. They imagine it will arrive as a powerful sense of certainty or relief. More often, safety feels much quieter than that. It’s feeling a little scared but sensing there’s enough solidity in the relationship that you can be yourself and express your true feelings.

Part of what creates emotional safety is something psychologists call “emotional attunement.” Although many people have heard the term, fewer understand what it actually means. Emotional attunement is the experience of feeling emotionally understood by another person. It happens when someone notices that something has shifted inside you and responds with curiosity rather than criticism, presence rather than avoidance, and interest rather than dismissal.

Imagine you have had a difficult day. An emotionally attuned partner might notice that you seem quieter than usual and ask, "You seem a little off today. Is something going on?" They are not trying to fix you. They are not trying to read your mind. They are communicating something equally important: "I notice you. Your experience matters to me."

Over time, these moments of attunement teach the nervous system that emotions can exist within relationships without threatening the relationship itself. That is a profoundly different experience from relationships in which emotions are ignored, mocked, minimized, punished, or met with withdrawal. Individuals who practice emotional attunement may have secure attachment. Studies suggest that secure attachment is associated with greater emotional flexibility and healthier responses to relational stress, helping individuals remain connected to themselves and others during difficult moments.1,2

The same dynamics show up in sexuality. Many people assume desire is determined by attraction alone. In reality, a nervous system that feels unsafe often struggles to relax into pleasure, vulnerability, and connection. This is one reason sexual difficulties are frequently more complex than questions of libido, attraction, or technique. A body that is historically used to and bracing for criticism, rejection, conflict, or abandonment often has difficulty fully opening to intimacy.

When people begin to experience emotional safety, they often notice subtle shifts. They may feel less pressure to perform, manage, or earn their place in the relationship. They may find themselves able to express disagreement without fearing abandonment. They may spend less time trying to decode another person's tone of voice or wondering what a delayed text message means. Instead of constantly focusing on the other person's reactions, they remain more connected to their own thoughts, feelings, and bodily sensations.

People are sometimes surprised when I tell them that safety often feels less dramatic than anxiety. Safety does not usually create the same rush as uncertainty, which is really another word for anxiety. Safety does not produce the same preoccupation that can accompany inconsistent attention. There is less urgency. Less chasing. Less monitoring.

For individuals who have historically associated intensity with connection, this can feel unfamiliar. Sometimes people mistake this unfamiliarity for a lack of chemistry. In reality, what may be missing is not attraction. It may be anxiety.

One of the most important misconceptions about safety is that it comes entirely from other people. Healthy relationships certainly matter. Choosing emotionally available partners matters. Learning to recognize unhealthy dynamics matters. But safety is also something we learn to cultivate within ourselves.

Part of healing involves developing the capacity to notice what is happening inside us without immediately abandoning ourselves in response. It means learning to recognize our own emotional experience, identify our own boundaries, and remain connected to ourselves even when relationships become challenging.

If you are curious about your own experience of safety, consider the following questions:

• Do I feel more like myself or less like myself around this person?
• Can I express disagreement without fearing the relationship will end?
• Do I feel pressure to manage their emotions?
• Am I able to notice what is happening in my body, or am I focused entirely on what is happening in theirs?
• Do I feel relaxed, or am I constantly monitoring for what might happen next?

Many people spend years learning how to recognize danger. Healing involves developing an equally important skill: learning how to recognize safety when it arrives and allowing yourself to trust it long enough to let it change you.

item.title: How to Get Better at Anything: Influence, Leadership, and More
item.description:
Leadership

How to Get Better at Anything: Influence, Leadership, and More

Practice is overrated. Here’s what to do instead.

Posted June 25, 2026

Key points
  • When most people practice, they unwittingly repeat what they are already good at.
  • Performance improvement requires addressing the areas where you have most room to improve.
  • Experience does not equal expertise. Experience accrues automatically; expertise must be made deliberately.
You can improve dramatically with the right approach.
Source: Generated with AI: Codex / OpenAI

As a professor of leadership, I work with postgraduate business students and executive clients to make real improvements in their influence, leadership, and communication skills. When I start discussing how workplace performance improves, the audience tends to offer up “Practice makes perfect.” It’s a nice, simple statement, but it’s far from true. Doing something over and over again doesn’t necessarily make you any better at it.

Experience and Expertise Are Not the Same Thing

We routinely use the term "experience" as if it means "expertise." At work, someone with years of experience meeting customers, leading a team, or presenting ideas has had plenty of practice doing these things. We assume this means they are an expert because we conflate the terms involved. Instead, when experience and expertise are defined independently, experience is a relatively poor predictor of expertise.[1,2,3]

Neither Experience nor Practice Automatically Leads to Improvement

Experience does not automatically lead to improvement beyond a certain level because once we have the skills needed to achieve average performance in our jobs, we switch our focus from developing skills (methodology) to getting the job done (outcome).[4} Years of experience might make you feel as if you are learning new skills, but statistically significantly, you become more and more likely to rely on the same skills that have worked for you in the past.[5]

Dr. Anders Ericsson, a leading expert on expertise, offers a useful analogy.[6] A new tennis player practices all elements of play, including backhand and forehand. But once he or she feels ready to play matches, that player will naturally rely on what has worked for them in the past (e.g., strong forehand) and avoid what has not (e.g., weak backhand). As a result, the player's forehand becomes stronger and the backhand, weaker. That backhand skill is unlikely to improve, even in years of playing tennis, because the player is not trying to improve their backhand. They are trying to win.

At work, real skill practice is rare because our busy working lives leave neither time nor incentive to stop chasing outcomes and instead improve methodology. Even if we do find time to practice a skill, we can’t help drifting toward repeating the elements we are already good at. That’s because it’s more enjoyable than focusing on where we are weak. In a study of footballers, regular players found practice more fun and easier than expert players because the former simply repeated what they were good at, while the latter focused on where they had most room to improve.[7]

In summary, experience and practice don’t provide the improvements we seek, but there are approaches that deliver results.

How You Can Actually Improve: Step-by-Step

Drawing on work by Ericsson, his colleagues, and other researchers, we can identify powerful factors that drive performance improvement. Whether I am working with a room of MBA students or individual clients one-on-one, the better I can satisfy these conditions, the stronger the skill development I can enable in others.

  1. The learner must actively want to improve. Improvement takes work, not wishful thinking, so the learner must be motivated to make the effort required.
  2. Aim for small and regular over large and infrequent. Twenty minutes of walking three times a week beats one six-hour gym session that you never repeat. Skill development is essentially habit change, so start small if that helps you start now.
  3. Break the overall skill into specific parts. A common error is to set a vague goal such as “Improve at customer interaction.” Customer interaction must be broken into specific components, such as “Ask effective questions” and “Demonstrate active listening,” so that the actions required are clear and concrete.
  4. Work with an expert who uses an expert model (not personal opinion) to give feedback. The learner needs to picture what good looks like, and the model of “good” should be empirically validated as leading to the desired result. An expert uses the model to give systematic feedback that closes the gap between where the learner is and where they need to be.
  5. Start where you have the most room to improve. These are usually the skill components that you have been avoiding. Focused effort here will not only strengthen your overall skill, but it will also build confidence that you can improve.
  6. Practice in a "training zone" that has the same paradigms, but less risk. Airlines use flight simulators, so pilots build critical skills without risking real passengers or real aircraft. The more the training context matches the real-world environment—minus the risks—the more transferable those skills will be. Like a flight simulation, build client interaction skills while working with actors or peers, not live clients.
  7. Expect and embrace failure. If you are doing things you are not yet good at, you will fail. In the real world, you instinctively avoid failure; in the training zone, you should expect it. Embrace it as a sign you are on the right path.
  8. Repeat with refinement. Iteration is a crucial element of improvement. Each time you repeat the skill component, maintain what you are doing well, but refine what is not yet on target.

In summary, unless you are deliberately working to improve, chances are you are not improving; you are performing. Few people will get better on their own, but the right guidance and the right strategies can enable you to level up in ways that years of experience will not.
